method_note: In this session WebFetch could not reach pubmed/pmc/pubchem/uniprot/federalregister/rcsb, and curl was also blocked, so no source page was opened directly. Every claim below was checked with WebSearch. 'quote' fields are passages from search-engine extracts of the cited page, not text copied from the page itself. Before anything is published, confirm each quote against the live page. The quote_verification field says how strong each one is: 'search_extract_verbatim' means the search tool presented the passage as quoted text; 'search_paraphrase' means it was a summary.
compliance_note: Several source papers use treatment/disease language. Do not carry it into EQ copy (org rule: no treat/cure/diagnose/prevent claims).

claim: NAD+ is a coenzyme for redox (electron-transfer) reactions, which makes it central to cellular energy metabolism, mitochondrial energy metabolism included.
quote: NAD+ is a coenzyme for redox reactions, making it central to energy metabolism.
quote_verification: search_extract_verbatim (abstract wording reported for the Nature and PubMed pages)
source: Covarrubias AJ, Perrone R, Grozio A, Verdin E. NAD+ metabolism and its roles in cellular processes during ageing. Nat Rev Mol Cell Biol 2021;22:119-141. PMID 33353981
status: VERIFIED

claim: Besides its redox role, NAD+ is a cofactor/substrate that non-redox enzymes consume, including sirtuins, CD38 and PARPs. The reactions release nicotinamide, and the NAD+ has to be resynthesized.
quote: NAD+ is also an essential cofactor for non-redox NAD+-dependent enzymes, including sirtuins, CD38 and poly(ADP-ribose) polymerases.
source: Covarrubias et al. 2021 Nat Rev Mol Cell Biol (same abstract)
status: VERIFIED

claim: Human, cross-sectional data: in non-sun-exposed pelvic skin from 49 people (newborns plus patients aged 15-77), NAD+ levels correlated negatively with age in both males (r = -0.706) and females (r = -0.537). Caveats: this is a single correlational study in one tissue. A 2025 Nature Metabolism review notes that a human age-related NAD+ decline 'has been consistently observed in only a limited number of studies', and a 2021 review (PMC8747183) asks whether the decline is a 'universal truth or confounded consensus'.
quote: A strong negative correlation was observed between NAD(+) levels and age in both males (p = 0.001; r = -0.706) and females (p = 0.01; r = -0.537).
source: Massudi H et al. Age-associated changes in oxidative stress and NAD+ metabolism in human tissue. PLoS One 2012;7:e42357
species_tissue: Human; non-sun-exposed (pelvic) skin from surgical tissue
status: VERIFIED (with caveat that the evidence is limited)

claim: In mice, CD38 protein levels and enzyme activity rise with age in several tissues, and CD38 is required for the age-related NAD+ decline and mitochondrial dysfunction, partly through SIRT3. In CD38-knockout mice the age-related NAD+ decline was largely prevented. This evidence is mostly mouse and cell work. A later study (PubMed 33199925) found CD38 induced in immune cells during ageing.
quote: CD38 protein levels rose in several tissues with age, along with its enzymatic activity, while SIRT1 and PARP1 did not show the same pattern.
quote_verification: search_paraphrase (from the Cell Metab commentary 'Why NAD+ Declines during Aging: It's Destroyed'). No verbatim abstract quote was obtained.
source: Camacho-Pereira J et al. CD38 dictates age-related NAD decline and mitochondrial dysfunction through an SIRT3-dependent mechanism. Cell Metab 2016;23:1127-1139. doi:10.1016/j.cmet.2016.05.006
status: VERIFIED (substance confirmed; the quote is a paraphrase, so re-quote the abstract before publishing)

claim: Small human trials show oral NAD+ precursors raise blood NAD+. Trammell 2016: single NR doses of 100, 300 and 1,000 mg in 12 healthy subjects gave dose-dependent increases in the blood NAD+ metabolome. In a one-person pilot, blood-cell NAD+ rose as much as 2.7-fold. Martens 2018: 1,000 mg/day NR for 6 weeks in 30 healthy middle-aged and older adults (randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover) was well tolerated and raised blood cellular NAD+. A separate NIAGEN trial (PMC6611812) reported whole-blood NAD+ increases of 22%, 51% and 142% at 100/300/1000 mg. An NMN trial (PMC9036060) also reported raised blood NAD+. Note: some of these trials were industry-funded (ChromaDex).
quote: single doses of 100, 300 and 1,000 mg of NR produce dose-dependent increases in the blood NAD+ metabolome in the first clinical trial of NR pharmacokinetics in humans
source: Trammell SAJ et al. Nat Commun 2016;7:12948 (PMID 27721479); Martens CR et al. Nat Commun 2018;9:1286
status: VERIFIED. A ~60% PBMC figure sometimes attributed to Martens could not be confirmed; do not use it.

claim: Raising NAD+ has shown limited and inconclusive functional benefit in humans, even though it is biologically active and preclinical data look promising.
quote: Although preclinical studies support NAD+ precursors as a promising strategy for healthy ageing, human clinical trials have shown limited efficacy.
source: NAD+ precursor supplementation in human ageing: clinical evidence and challenges. Nat Metab 2025;7:1974-1990. PMID 41083806. Corroborated by a 2025 PRISMA systematic review (PMID 41655607): 'clinical effectiveness for anti-aging or wellness outcomes remains inconclusive'.
status: VERIFIED

claim: No published human studies of intranasal NAD+ were found. The evidence is animal-only: in a rat transient focal ischemia model, intranasal NAD+ (10 mg/kg, given 2 h after ischemia onset) raised brain NAD+ and reduced infarct size and neurological deficits, while intranasal nicotinamide did not. Other rodent work includes a mouse ischemia study and a rat TBI study (20 mg/kg intranasal).
quote: Intranasal NAD+ delivery significantly increased NAD+ contents in the brains
source: Ying W et al. Intranasal administration with NAD+ profoundly decreases brain injury in a rat model of transient focal ischemia. Front Biosci 2007;12:2728-34
status: VERIFIED that animal-only data exist. Human intranasal NAD+ data: NONE FOUND (searched with extended mode).

claim: IV NAD+ tolerability depends on rate and evidence is limited. Grant 2019 (n=11 healthy males; 8 NAD+, 3 saline; 3 umol/min for 6 h) reported no adverse events at that slow rate. A 2026 retrospective clinic chart review (n=6 NAD+, 500 mg IV on 4 consecutive days) found all six reported symptoms during infusion, including abdominal cramping, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, raised heart rate, throat pain, congestion and chest pressure. Symptoms ended when the infusion stopped and led participants to slow the rate. A 2026 review lists nausea, abdominal discomfort, flushing, cramping and chest pressure, particularly at faster rates. Intranasal irritation: no data found.
quote: these adverse experiences ceased immediately upon infusion completion, although did cause participants to reduce infusion rate
source: Intravenous infusion of NAD+ versus NR: a retrospective tolerability pilot study in a real-world setting. Front Aging 2026 (doi 10.3389/fragi.2026.1652582); Grant R et al. Front Aging Neurosci 2019;11:257
status: PARTIALLY VERIFIED. 'Flushing' appears only in the 2026 review list and in clinic blogs, not in the primary studies. The 2026 study's authors are affiliated with the infusion-clinic chain. Intranasal irritation is UNVERIFIED: no source found.

claim: The molecular formula of NAD+ (neutral free acid, PubChem CID 5892) is C21H27N7O14P2, with MW ~663.4 g/mol. The charged NAD+ anion record (CID 15938971, C21H26N7O14P2-) lists ~662.4. NAD+ is a dinucleotide (two nucleotides joined by a pyrophosphate), not a peptide.
quote: formula C21H27N7O14P2 and a molecular weight of 663.43 g/mol
quote_verification: search_paraphrase (compound-data page citing CID 5892; RCSB ligand NAD lists 663.425)
source: PubChem CID 5892; RCSB PDB ligand NAD
status: VERIFIED (via secondary mirrors; the PubChem page itself was not reachable)

claim: Naltrexone (PubChem CID 5360515) is C20H23NO4, MW ~341.4 g/mol. It is a small molecule (opioid antagonist), not a peptide. The HCl salt is ~377.9 g/mol.
quote: Average Molecular Weight 341.4009
quote_verification: search_extract_verbatim (HMDB HMDB0014842; PubChemLite confirms CID 5360515 = C20H23NO4)
source: PubChem CID 5360515; HMDB0014842
status: VERIFIED (via mirrors)

claim: MOTS-c is a 16-amino-acid peptide encoded by a short open reading frame (51 bp) within the mitochondrial 12S rRNA gene.
quote: MOTSC is encoded as a 51-bp short open reading frame (sORF) in the mitochondrial 12S rRNA
quote_verification: search_paraphrase (Lee 2015 / PMC copies). The count of 16 aa is consistent: 51 bp = 16 codons + stop.
source: Lee C et al. The mitochondrial-derived peptide MOTS-c promotes metabolic homeostasis and reduces obesity and insulin resistance. Cell Metab 2015;21:443-454
status: VERIFIED

claim: In cells and mice, MOTS-c raises endogenous AICAR and activates AMPK, increasing glucose utilization and fatty acid oxidation. In mice it prevented diet-induced obesity and insulin resistance. Under metabolic stress it moves to the nucleus in an AMPK-dependent manner (Kim 2018). Mechanism data are mouse/cell only.
quote: increased glucose utilization and fatty acid oxidation, decreased oxidative phosphorylation, increased endogenous AICAR levels, and AMPK activation
source: Lee C et al. Cell Metab 2015; Kim KH et al. Cell Metab 2018 (PMC6185997)
status: VERIFIED

claim: In 10 sedentary healthy young men doing a single stationary-cycling session, skeletal-muscle MOTS-c rose 11.9-fold after exercise (18.9-fold after 4 h rest). Circulating MOTS-c rose ~1.6-fold during and ~1.5-fold after exercise. This was a small, all-male, single-session study.
quote: endogenous MOTS-c levels in skeletal muscle significantly increased after exercise (11.9-fold) and remained elevated after a 4-hour rest (18.9-fold)
quote_verification: search_extract_verbatim (bioRxiv preprint wording; cohort details confirmed for the Nat Commun version)
source: Reynolds JC et al. MOTS-c is an exercise-induced mitochondrial-encoded regulator of age-dependent physical decline and muscle homeostasis. Nat Commun 2021;12:470
status: VERIFIED (check the fold-change figures against the published version's figures)

claim: Human data are limited and mixed. D'Souza 2020 (men only; young, middle-aged and older groups) found plasma MOTS-c lower with age while skeletal-muscle MOTS-c was higher with age. Reviews cite ~11% and ~21% higher blood levels in young vs middle-aged and old. A 2024 athlete study found no significant age-group difference.
quote: plasma MOTS-c levels are reduced with age while muscle levels are increased
source: D'Souza RF et al. Increased expression of the mitochondrial derived peptide, MOTS-c, in skeletal muscle of healthy aging men is associated with myofiber composition. Aging (Albany NY) 2020;12:5244
status: VERIFIED, with correction: the decline is in plasma only; muscle MOTS-c increases with age. The 11%/21% figures come from reviews and were not checked against the primary data.

claim: No peer-reviewed human trial of native MOTS-c administration was found. The only human interventional data are for CB4211, a modified MOTS-c analog from CohBar (Phase 1a/1b, NCT03998514; 25 mg SC daily for 4 weeks in the 1b portion). Topline results exist only as a 2021 company press release: well tolerated, no SAEs, mostly mild-moderate injection-site reactions. Efficacy signals were small (liver fat -5.03% vs placebo -4.88%). No posted registry results or peer-reviewed paper were found.
quote: CB4211 was well-tolerated and appeared safe with no serious adverse events.
source: CohBar press release, 10 Aug 2021 (GlobeNewswire)
tier: T2 (analog, unpublished topline only); native MOTS-c in humans: none
status: VERIFIED that native MOTS-c has no published human trials. The CB4211 data are non-peer-reviewed, and sources disagree on enrollment (65 vs 88).

claim: KPV is the tripeptide Lys-Pro-Val (3 aa), the C-terminal residues 11-13 of alpha-MSH.
quote: the minimum sequence required for anti-inflammatory activity of α-MSH is the C-terminal tripeptide
source: Dalmasso G et al. PepT1-mediated tripeptide KPV uptake reduces intestinal inflammation. Gastroenterology 2008
status: VERIFIED

claim: GHK is the tripeptide glycyl-L-histidyl-L-lysine (3 aa). GHK-Cu is its copper(II) complex. It was first isolated from human albumin/plasma by Pickart in 1973.
quote: GHK is a tripeptide composed of glycine, L-histidine, and L-lysine. The peptide exhibits a high affinity for copper (II), forming the bioactive complex GHK-Cu
source: Systematic review of GHK-Cu in topical microneedle delivery (PMC13604022); Pickart & Margolina 2012 (PMC3359723)
status: VERIFIED

claim: Oxytocin is a nonapeptide (9 aa): Cys-Tyr-Ile-Gln-Asn-Cys-Pro-Leu-Gly-NH2, with a Cys1-Cys6 disulfide forming a 6-residue ring.
quote: Cysteine residues form a disulfide bond to create a cyclic six amino acid ring for both neuropeptides.
quote_verification: search_extract_verbatim; the sequence Cys-Tyr-Ile-Gln-Asn-Cys-Pro-Leu-Gly-NH2 is reported across sources
source: PMC5013270 (oxytocin/vasopressin measurement paper); Lee HJ et al. Oxytocin: the great facilitator of life (PMC2689929)
status: VERIFIED

claim: Bremelanotide (PT-141; Vyleesi) is Ac-Nle-cyclo[Asp-His-D-Phe-Arg-Trp-Lys]-OH. That is 7 residues (including non-proteinogenic norleucine and D-Phe), cyclized by an Asp-Lys lactam bridge, as a cyclic alpha-MSH analog. Free base C50H68N14O10, MW ~1025.2.
quote: Ac-Nle-cyclo-(Asp-His-D-Phe-Arg-Trp-Lys-OH)
quote_verification: search_extract_verbatim (Vyleesi label text as reproduced on RxList)
source: Vyleesi (bremelanotide) prescribing information, NDA 210557
status: VERIFIED (better to swap the URL for the FDA label / DailyMed; FDA hosts were not reachable here). Caveat: it is called a 7-'amino acid' peptide even though Nle and D-Phe are non-standard.

claim: BPC-157 is a synthetic 15-amino-acid peptide (pentadecapeptide), GEPPPGKPADDAGLV, MW ~1419.5 Da, described as derived from a gastric juice protein. It is not approved for human use by any regulator.
quote: synthetic pentadecapeptide derived from a gastric protein fragment
quote_verification: search_extract_verbatim (PMC13210877); sequence and MW from PMC11859134
source: BPC-157 as an Investigational Peptide Therapeutic (PMC13210877); PMC11859134
status: VERIFIED

claim: MOTS-c is 16 amino acids (MRWQEMGYIFYPRKLR per Lee 2015; the sequence itself was not re-verified here).
quote: MOTS-c ... a 16-amino-acid peptide encoded in the mitochondrial genome
source: Lee C et al. Cell Metab 2015
status: VERIFIED (count); sequence string not verified, so omit it from the graphic or check it

claim: Tirzepatide is a 39-amino-acid linear peptide based on the GIP sequence, a dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonist. MW ~4813.5 Da, C225H348N48O68. It also carries a C20 fatty-diacid moiety (not verified here).
quote: 39 amino acids ... molecular weight of about 4813.53 Da and the formula C225H348N48O68
quote_verification: search_paraphrase of Mounjaro label DESCRIPTION section (RxList/GlobalRPh mirror)
source: Mounjaro (tirzepatide) prescribing information, Section 11 Description
status: VERIFIED (count); fatty-diacid detail UNVERIFIED. Note: 39 is under FDA's 40-aa protein threshold, so it regulates as a peptide/drug.

claim: Human insulin has 51 amino acids in two chains: A chain 21 and B chain 30. It has three disulfides (A7-B7, A20-B19 interchain; A6-A11 intrachain). Proinsulin is 86 aa.
quote: The insulin molecule consists of 51 amino acids arranged in two chains, an A chain (21 amino acids) and B chain (30 amino acids).
source: Endotext: Insulin - Pharmacology, Therapeutic Regimens and Principles of Intensive Insulin Therapy (NCBI Bookshelf NBK278938)
status: VERIFIED. Under the 2020 FDA rule, insulin counts as a 'protein' because its chains are summed (51 > 40).

claim: The mature human serum albumin chain (UniProt P02768) is 585 residues (Asp25-Leu609). The 609-aa precursor includes a signal peptide (1-18) and a propeptide (19-24).
quote: serum albumin chain at 585 residues
quote_verification: search_paraphrase (RCSB PDB 7FFR mapped to UniProt P02768; OriGene recombinant Asp25-Leu609 citing P02768)
source: UniProtKB P02768 (ALBU_HUMAN)
status: VERIFIED (585 is consistent across two mirrors; UniProt itself was unreachable). The propeptide boundary was not confirmed, so cite only 585 mature / 609 precursor.

claim: FDA final rule (85 FR 10057, Feb 21 2020): a 'protein' is any alpha amino acid polymer with a specific, defined sequence that is greater than 40 amino acids. A peptide is 40 or fewer. For multi-chain molecules such as insulin the chains are summed. Chemically synthesized polypeptides over 40 aa are also proteins. Codified at 21 CFR 600.3(h)(6).
quote: the term protein as any alpha amino acid polymer with a specific, defined sequence that is greater than 40 amino acids in size
source: FDA, Definition of the Term 'Biological Product', Final Rule, 85 Fed. Reg. 10057 (Feb. 21, 2020), Docket FDA-2018-N-2732
status: VERIFIED. Wording note: the rule defines 'protein' (>40 aa) and treats peptides as ≤40 aa. Present the 'peptide = 40 or fewer' line as following from the protein definition, not as a separately codified peptide definition. Confirm the exact 21 CFR 600.3 text before quoting it in compliance material.

claim: Full-length thymosin beta-4 is 43 aa (count not re-verified here). 'TB-500' as sold has been analytically identified as the N-terminally acetylated 17-23 fragment Ac-LKKTETQ, which is 7 aa. Caveat: vendors often conflate TB-500 with full-length Tβ4, and product identity and purity vary. Tβ4 is on the WADA prohibited list.
quote: Synthesis and characterization of the N-terminal acetylated 17-23 fragment of thymosin beta 4 identified in TB-500, a product suspected to possess doping potential
source: Esposito S et al. Drug Test Anal 2012 (PMID 22962027); Ho EN et al. equine doping control of TB-500 (PMID 23084823); orthopaedic review describing TB-500 as a 'distinct seven-amino-acid fragment often conflated with full-length thymosin beta-4' (PMID 42937313)
status: VERIFIED (7-aa Ac-LKKTETQ). The 43-aa full-length figure was not re-verified in this session; confirm it via UniProt P62328.
